topic.name: Periodicity of Chemical Properties of the Elements in Period 3

subtopics.name: Acid/Base Behaviour of the Period 3 Oxides & Hydroxides
Electronegativity & Bonding of the Period 3 Elements

parts.problem_md:
The oxides of Period 3 elements (sodium to phosphorus) show a transition from ionic to covalent character. This affects both their acid–base nature and their behaviour in water.

Which row gives the correct properties of the given oxides?

|   | Oxide | Type of structure | Acid–base nature | Result of adding to water |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | MgO | Giant ionic | Basic | Forms a solution with pH ≈ 9 |
| **B** | Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> | Giant ionic | Amphoteric | Forms a solution with pH ≈ 7 |
| **C** | SiO<sub>2</sub> | Giant covalent | Acidic | Forms a solution with pH ≈ 2 |
| **D** | P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> | Simple molecular | Acidic | Forms a solution with pH ≈ 13 |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Across Period 3, the oxides change from **giant ionic** (metals) to **giant covalent** or **simple molecular** (non-metals).
- **MgO** is a giant ionic oxide with basic properties.

  - It is sparingly soluble in water but reacts to form magnesium hydroxide, giving a weakly alkaline solution of approximately pH 8–9.

**B** is incorrect as although Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is amphoteric, it is **insoluble** in water and does not produce a solution at pH ≈ 7.

**C** is incorrect as SiO<sub>2</sub> is an acidic oxide with a giant covalent structure. It is **insoluble** in water and does not form an acidic solution.

**D** is incorrect as P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> reacts with water to form phosphoric acid, giving a solution of low pH (approximately 1–2), not pH ≈ 13.

parts.problem_md:
Mohr's salt is a pale green crystalline solid which is soluble in water. It contains two cations, of which one is Fe<sup>2+</sup> and one anion which is SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>.

The second cation was determined by heating solid Mohr's salt with solid sodium hydroxide, and a colourless gas was evolved. The gas readily dissolved in water giving an alkaline solution.

A grey-green solid residue was also formed, which was insoluble in water.

Which row correctly identifies the grey-green residue and the colourless gas?

|   | **Residue** | **Gas** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub> | NH<sub>3</sub> |
| **B** | Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub> | SO<sub>2</sub> |
| **C** | Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | NH<sub>3</sub> |
| **D** | Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | SO<sub>2</sub> |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- A colourless gas that dissolves in water to give an **alkaline solution** is **ammonia (NH**<sub>**3**</sub>**)**, so the second cation is NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.
- NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> reacts with OH<sup>-</sup> to release ammonia:

NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup> $\rightarrow$ NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

- The Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions in Mohr's salt react with OH<sup>-</sup> to form **iron(II) hydroxide**, an insoluble grey-green solid:

Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2OH<sup>-</sup> (aq) $\rightarrow$ Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s)

- Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is also formed but it is a **white, soluble** solid

  - This does not account for the grey-green insoluble residue.

**B** is incorrect as SO<sub>2</sub> is not produced. NaOH reacts with the NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> cation, not with SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is a **white, soluble** solid. It cannot be the grey-green insoluble residue.

**D** is incorrect as the gas produced is NH<sub>3</sub> (dissolves to give alkaline solution), not SO<sub>2</sub> (which dissolves to give an acidic solution).

> **[exam-tip]**
> The colour of the residue is a key identifier:
> 
> - Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub> is grey-green
> - Fe(OH)<sub>3</sub> is rust-coloured (orange-brown).
> 
> Knowing these colours allows you to eliminate options quickly.
> 
> The alkaline gas is always NH<sub>3</sub> and is the only common colourless gas from Period 3 reactions with NaOH that gives an alkaline solution in water.

parts.problem_md:
An element **X** reacts according to the following sequence.

**X** $\overset{\mathrm{burns} \mathrm{in}O_{2}}{\rightarrow}$ white solid `rightwards arrow with HCl space open parentheses aq close parentheses on top` solution `rightwards arrow with NaOH thin space open parentheses aq close parentheses on top` white precipitate `rightwards arrow with excess space NaOH thin space open parentheses aq close parentheses on top` solution

What could be element **X**?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- When aluminium burns in oxygen, **aluminium oxide** is formed:

4Al (s) + 3O<sub>2</sub> (g) $\rightarrow$ 2Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (s)

- Aluminium oxide is **amphoteric** as it reacts with both acids and bases.
- Aluminium oxide with hydrochloric acid produces aluminium chloride:

Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (s) + 6HCl (aq) $\rightarrow$ 2AlCl<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

- Adding sodium hydroxide to aluminium chloride solution produces **insoluble aluminium hydroxide**:

AlCl<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 3NaOH (aq) $\rightarrow$ Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> (s) + 3NaCl (aq)

- In **excess** sodium hydroxide, the aluminium hydroxide dissolves to form the soluble aluminate ion:

Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> (s) + NaOH (aq) $\rightarrow$ Na<sup>+</sup>[Al(OH)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>-</sup> (aq)

**A** is incorrect as Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> formed when magnesium chloride reacts with sodium hydroxide does **not** dissolve in excess NaOH. Magnesium hydroxide has no amphoteric properties.

**B** is incorrect as SiO<sub>2</sub> is a **covalent** compound with **no basic properties**. It cannot react with hydrochloric acid, so the sequence cannot proceed.

**D** is incorrect as P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> is a **covalent** compound with **no basic properties**. It cannot react with hydrochloric acid.

parts.problem_md:
When solution **X** is titrated against hydrochloric acid, a neutralisation reaction occurs.

Which of the following hydroxides is **not** solution **X**?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- For a hydroxide to react with hydrochloric acid in a neutralisation reaction, it must act as a **base**.

  - Phosphorus does not form a simple hydroxide.
- The compound is **phosphoric acid** (H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>), which is itself an **acid**.

  - It donates H<sup>+</sup> ions in solution.
- An acid cannot neutralise another acid, so H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> does not react with hydrochloric acid in a neutralisation reaction.

**A** is incorrect as Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> acts as a base and reacts with HCl:

Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl $\rightarrow$ MgCl<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

**B** is incorrect as Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> acts as a base and reacts with HCl:

Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> + 3HCl $\rightarrow$ AlCl<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O

**C** is incorrect as NaOH is a strong base and readily reacts with HCl:

NaOH + HCl $\rightarrow$ NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>O

parts.problem_md:
Bacteria in swimming pools are killed by adding aqueous sodium chlorate (I), NaOCl. This reacts with water to produce HOCl molecules which can breach the bacteria cell wall and kill the bacteria. The reaction below shows the reaction with water:

OCl<sup>–</sup> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O  $\underset{}{\rightleftharpoons}$  OH<sup>–</sup> (aq) + HOCl (aq)

Under the sun’s UV rays, the OCl<sup>–</sup> ion is broken down by ultra-violet light:

OCl<sup>–</sup> (aq) + uv light $\rightarrow$ Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g)

Which method would maintain the highest concentration of HOCl (aq)?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Increasing the pool water acidity adds H<sup>+</sup> ions, which **reduces the concentration of OH**<sup>**-**</sup>** ions**.
- By Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium shifts to the **right** (forward direction) to oppose the decrease in OH<sup>-</sup>, producing more HOCl.
- Increasing [HOCl] maintains the pool's bactericidal effectiveness.

**A** is incorrect as Cl<sup>-</sup> ions are not a component of this equilibrium, so adding them has no effect on [HOCl].

**C** is incorrect as none of the gases in air (O<sub>2</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>) appear in this equilibrium, so bubbling air through the water has no effect.

**D** is incorrect as adding OH<sup>-</sup> ions shifts the equilibrium to the **left** (reverse direction), opposing the increase in OH<sup>-</sup> and reducing [HOCl].

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: Add a solution containing chloride ions.

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: Add a solution of hydroxide ion.

parts.problem_md:
G and J are oxides of different Period 3 elements.

If one mole of J is added to water, the solution formed is neutralised by exactly one mole of G.

What could be the identities of G and J?

|   | **G** | **J** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Na<sub>2</sub>O | SO<sub>3</sub> |
| **B** | Na<sub>2</sub>O | P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> |
| **C** | Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> | SO<sub>3</sub> |
| **D** | Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> | P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When SO<sub>3</sub> is added to water, it produces **sulfuric acid**:

SO<sub>3</sub> (l) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) $\rightarrow$ H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq)

- Na<sub>2</sub>O is a basic oxide. One mole of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is neutralised by exactly one mole of Na<sub>2</sub>O:

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + Na<sub>2</sub>O $\rightarrow$ Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

- Sodium sulfate forms a neutral solution (pH 7).

**B** is incorrect as P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> reacts with water to produce **four** moles of phosphoric acid (4H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>). One mole of Na<sub>2</sub>O cannot neutralise four moles of H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>.

**C** is incorrect as the molar ratio of Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> to H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is **1:3** (to form Al<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>), not 1:1. One mole of SO<sub>3</sub> produces only one mole of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, which is not sufficient to fully neutralise one mole of Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.

**D** is incorrect as P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> produces four moles of H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, which cannot be neutralised by one mole of Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> in a 1:1 ratio.

parts.problem_md:
Silicon reacts with chlorine to produce silicon tetrachloride.

How many moles of chlorine are needed to react with 1 mole of silicon?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Silicon has **4 valence electrons** and forms 4 covalent bonds; chlorine has **7 valence electrons** and forms 1 covalent bond.

- One silicon atom bonds with 4 chlorine atoms to form SiCl<sub>4</sub>.
- Since chlorine exists as diatomic Cl<sub>2</sub>, the balanced equation is:

Si + 2Cl<sub>2</sub> $\rightarrow$ SiCl<sub>4</sub>

- Therefore, **2 moles of Cl**<sub>**2**</sub> are required per mole of silicon.

![Dot-and-cross diagram showing silicon bonded to four chlorine atoms in SiCl4](assets/001-dot-and-cross-diagram-showing-silicon-bonded-to-.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as 3 moles of Cl<sub>2</sub> would give SiCl<sub>6</sub>, which silicon cannot form (Period 3 elements beyond the 3s and 3p cannot expand their octet at this level).

**C** is incorrect as 4 refers to the number of chlorine *atoms* in SiCl<sub>4</sub>, not the number of Cl<sub>2</sub> molecules. Since Cl<sub>2</sub> is diatomic, only 2 moles are needed.

**D** is incorrect as 5 moles of Cl<sub>2</sub> would give SiCl<sub>10</sub>, which is not a known compound.

parts.problem_md:
The labels had become detached from four bottles in the laboratory. A student realised that the contents of one of them could easily be identified because in the addition of water it would **not** give fumes of hydrogen chloride.

Which did **not** give the HCl fumes?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- **Magnesium chloride** is an ionic compound and dissociates into Mg<sup>2+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions when dissolved in water.

- No reaction occurs because neither ion reacts with water.

- The chloride ion cannot extract H<sup>+</sup> from water to form hydrochloric acid:

MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s) $\rightarrow$ Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq)

**A** is incorrect as aluminium chloride has significant **covalent character** and reacts with water to produce hydrochloric acid fumes:

AlCl<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O $\rightarrow$ Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> + 3HCl

**B** is incorrect as silicon tetrachloride is a **covalent molecule** that reacts readily with water to produce hydrochloric acid:

SiCl<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O $\rightarrow$ SiO<sub>2</sub> + 4HCl

**C** is incorrect as phosphorus(V) chloride is a covalent molecule that reacts with water to produce hydrochloric acid:

PCl<sub>5</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O $\rightarrow$ H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> + 5HCl

parts.problem_md: Which observations are made when a sample of phosphorus(V) chloride, PCl<sub>5</sub>, is added to a beaker of water?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Phosphorus(V) chloride (PCl<sub>5</sub>) is a **covalent solid**.

- When added to water, it undergoes a violent hydrolysis reaction producing hydrogen chloride gas and phosphoric(V) acid:

PCl<sub>5</sub> (s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l) $\rightarrow$ H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + 5HCl (g)

- The HCl gas meets atmospheric moisture to produce visible **steamy white fumes**.
- All products are soluble or gaseous, so no precipitate forms.

**A** is incorrect as the reaction between PCl<sub>5</sub> and water is vigorous, producing steamy HCl fumes.

**C** is incorrect as no precipitate forms and all products are either soluble (H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>) or gaseous (HCl).

**D** is incorrect as the only observation is steamy fumes of HCl. No white precipitate is produced.

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: Steamy fumes is the only observation.

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: A white precipitate is the only observation.

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: Steamy fumes and a white precipitate are both observed.

parts.problem_md: What happens to the pH of water when magnesium oxide is dissolved into it?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The oxides of Period 3 are:

  - **Basic** on the left-hand side (Na and Mg).
  - **Acidic** on the right-hand side (Si, P, S and Cl).
  - Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is **amphoteric** (can act as both an acid and a base).

- MgO is a **basic oxide** as it contains oxide ions (O<sup>2-</sup>) that react with water to produce hydroxide ions:

MgO (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) $\rightarrow$ Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq)

- The ionic equation is:

O<sup>2-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) $\rightarrow$ 2OH<sup>-</sup> (aq)

- The resulting Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> solution is alkaline (pH ~9), so the pH **increases**.

**A** is incorrect as MgO is a basic oxide, not an acidic one.

**B** is incorrect as MgO is basic and adding it to water increases (not decreases) the pH.

**D** is incorrect as MgO does react with water to form Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>, raising the pH above 7.

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: pH increases, because MgO is acidic.

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: pH decreases, because MgO is basic.

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: pH increases, because MgO is basic.

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: Nothing happens because MgO is neutral.

parts.problem_md:
Which row gives the correct order of the decreasing melting points of the four chlorides shown?

|   | **Highest melting point    **$\rightarrow$**  Lowest melting point** |   |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | HCl | S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> | CCl<sub>4</sub> | MgCl<sub>2</sub> |
| **B** | HCl | CCl<sub>4</sub> | S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> | MgCl<sub>2</sub> |
| **C** | MgCl<sub>2</sub> | CCl<sub>4</sub> | S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> | HCl |
| **D** | CCl<sub>4</sub> | S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> | HCl | MgCl<sub>2</sub> |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Magnesium chloride has the highest melting point because it forms a **giant ionic lattice**.

  - Strong electrostatic attractions between Mg<sup>2+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions extend throughout the lattice, so a large amount of energy is required to overcome these forces when the solid melts.
- CCl<sub>4</sub>, S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, and HCl are **simple covalent molecules**.

  - So, the forces between molecules are much weaker than ionic bonds.
- CCl<sub>4</sub> is **non-polar** because of its symmetrical tetrahedral shape.

  - So, the only intermolecular forces present are **instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces**.
- S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> is **polar**.

  - So, it experiences **permanent dipole-permanent dipole (pd-pd) interactions** as well as id-id forces.
- However, CCl<sub>4</sub> has a **larger molecular mass** (154 vs 135 g mol<sup>-1</sup>)

  - This gives it stronger id-id forces, so CCl<sub>4</sub> has the higher melting point of the two.
- HCl is also a **simple covalent molecule** with pd-pd interactions and id-id forces, but these intermolecular forces are weak.

  - As a result, HCl is a **gas at room temperature** and has a very low melting point.

parts.problem_md: Chlorides of Period 3 elements are dissolved in water. Which statement is correct?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Both **MgCl**<sub>**2**</sub> and **NaCl** are ionic compounds that dissolve without altering [H<sup>+</sup>].
- Neither Mg<sup>2+</sup> nor Na<sup>+</sup> reacts with water, and Cl<sup>-</sup> does not extract H<sup>+</sup> from water molecules.
- So, both give neutral solutions (pH 7).

**A** is incorrect as MgCl<sub>2</sub> forms a **neutral** solution because Mg<sup>2+</sup> does not react with water to produce H<sup>+</sup> ions.

**C** is incorrect as SiCl<sub>4</sub> is a **covalent molecule** that hydrolyses in water to produce an acidic solution:

SiCl<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O $\rightarrow$ SiO<sub>2</sub> + 4HCl

**D** is incorrect as NaCl forms a **neutral** solution because Na<sup>+</sup> does not react with water to produce OH<sup>-</sup> ions.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common misconception is that MgCl<sub>2</sub> forms a slightly acidic solution because Mg<sup>2+</sup> is a small, highly charged cation.
> 
> At CIE IAL level, MgCl<sub>2</sub> is treated as forming a neutral solution. Only the chlorides of transition metals and aluminium (which form hydrated ions capable of donating H<sup>+</sup>) produce acidic solutions.

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: MgCl<sub>2</sub> forms an acidic solution because Mg<sup>2+</sup> reacts with water.

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: Both MgCl<sub>2</sub> and NaCl form neutral solutions.

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: SiCl<sub>4</sub> forms a neutral solution as it does not react with water.

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: NaCl forms an alkaline solution because Na<sup>+</sup> reacts with water.

parts.problem_md:
During the manufacture of steel, the impurity P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> is removed by reacting it with calcium oxide. The only product of this reaction is a salt, calcium phosphate (Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>).

In this reaction, how many moles of P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> will react with three moles of calcium oxide?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The balanced equation for this reaction is:

P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> + 6CaO $\rightarrow$ 2Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>

- The molar ratio of P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> : CaO = 1 : 6.

- Amount of P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> reacting with 3 mol CaO = 3 ÷ 6 = **0.5 mol**

**B** is incorrect as 1.5 mol results from using an incorrect 1:2 molar ratio rather than 1:6.

**C** is incorrect as a 1:1 ratio is not consistent with the balanced equation.

**D** is incorrect as 6 is the stoichiometric coefficient of CaO in the equation, not the amount of P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>.

parts.problem_md: Which properties do compounds of silicon and aluminium have in common?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- **Aluminium oxide** does not react with water because the oxide ion is too strongly attracted to the Al<sup>3+</sup> ion to be displaced.
- **Silicon dioxide** has a giant covalent structure with strong covalent bonds throughout, so it does not dissolve in water.
- Both Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> and SiO<sub>2</sub> are therefore **insoluble in water**.

**A** is incorrect as only Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is **amphoteric** (reacts with both acids and bases). SiO<sub>2</sub> is acidic only. It reacts with strong bases but not with acids.

**C** is incorrect as neither AlCl<sub>3</sub> nor SiCl<sub>4</sub> produces simple metal cations in solution. AlCl<sub>3</sub> reacts with water to form the hydrated aluminium ion [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>. SiCl<sub>4</sub> is a covalent molecule that hydrolyses and does not produce Si<sup>4+</sup> ions.

**D** is incorrect as only AlCl<sub>3</sub> has coordinate (dative) bonding. In the Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub> dimer, chlorine lone pairs are donated to aluminium. SiCl<sub>4</sub> has only polar covalent bonds.

![Structure of the Al2Cl6 dimer showing two AlCl3 units bridged by chlorine atoms with coordinate bonding, and tetrahedral geometry around each aluminium](assets/002-structure-of-the-al2cl6-dimer-showing-two-alcl3-.jpg)

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: Their oxides are insoluble in water.

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: Aqueous solutions of their chlorides contain aluminium or silicon cations.

parts.problem_md: Which graph shows the electronegativity of the elements Na, Mg, Al and Si, from Period 3, plotted against their first ionisation energies?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Electronegativity increases continuously from Na to Si as nuclear charge increases while the number of electron shells remains constant:

Na < Mg < Al < Si (continuous increase on y-axis).

- **First ionisation energy** is the energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms:

X (g) $\rightarrow$ X<sup>+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup>

- Na has the lowest first ionisation energy (lowest nuclear charge; outer electron is 3s<sup>1</sup>).
- Al has a *lower* first ionisation energy than Mg despite having one more proton.

  - Al's outer electron is in the 3p subshell, which is at a higher energy level and is shielded by the 3s<sup>2</sup> electrons, outweighing the extra nuclear charge.
- Si has the highest first ionisation energy of the four (3p<sup>2</sup>, highest nuclear charge).
- The correct graph shows electronegativity increasing continuously on the y-axis, and first ionisation energy in the order Na < Al < Mg < Si on the x-axis (dip at Al).

**B**, **C**, and **D** are incorrect as they show the wrong trend for electronegativity, miss the dip in first ionisation energy at aluminium, or invert the relative positions of Mg and Al.

parts.problem_md: Which graph correctly shows the relative melting points of period 3 elements plotted against their relative electronegativities?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

**Melting point:**

- Silicon has the highest melting point because it has a **giant covalent structure**.
- Many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it, requiring a large amount of energy.
- The melting points of the **metals** (Na, Mg, Al) increase across the period as more electrons are delocalised per atom (1 from Na, 2 from Mg, 3 from Al), strengthening the metallic bonding.
- Phosphorus (P<sub>4</sub>) and sulfur (S<sub>8</sub>) are **simple covalent molecules** with only id-id forces between molecules.
- S<sub>8</sub> has a higher melting point than P<sub>4</sub> because its larger molecular mass (256 vs 124 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) means stronger id-id forces.

![Graph showing relative melting points across Period 3 elements: low for Na, increasing for Mg and Al, peaking at Si, then lower for P and S with S above P, then falling for Cl and Ar; alongside steadily increasing electronegativity from Na to Cl](assets/003-graph-showing-relative-melting-points-across-per.jpg)

**Electronegativity:**

- Electronegativity **increases steadily across Period 3** because nuclear charge increases while the shielding remains approximately constant, so the attraction on bonding electrons increases.

parts.problem_md:
Non-metallic elements and their atoms can have the two following properties.

**Property 1:**     Has **no** paired 3p electrons

**Property 2:**     Has an oxide that can form a strong acid in water

Which ros shows the properties of phosphorus and sulfur?

|   | **Sulfur** | **Phosphorus** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 2 only | 1 and 2 |
| **B** | 1 and 2 | 2 only |
| **C** | 1 and 2 | 1 and 2 |
| **D** | 2 only | 1 only |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

**Sulfur**

- The electron configuration of sulfur is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>4</sup>.
- The 3p<sup>4</sup> configuration has **one pair** of 3p electrons, so sulfur does **not** satisfy Property 1.
- However, sulfur trioxide reacts with water to produce **sulfuric acid**, a **strong acid** that fully dissociates in aqueous solution:

SO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O $\rightarrow$ H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

- Therefore, sulfur satisfies **Property 2 only**.

**Phosphorus**

- The electron configuration of phosphorus is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>3</sup>.
- By Hund's rule, the three 3p electrons each occupy a **separate 3p orbital**, so phosphorus has **no paired 3p electrons** and satisfies Property 1. ![Electron configuration diagram for phosphorus showing three unpaired electrons each in a separate 3p orbital (3px, 3py, 3pz), with configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p3](assets/004-electron-configuration-diagram-for-phosphorus-sh.jpg)
- Phosphorus oxides (P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub> and P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>) produce only **weak acids** (H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>) that do not fully dissociate, so phosphorus does **not** satisfy Property 2.
- Therefore, phosphorus satisfies **Property 1 only**.

**A** is incorrect as phosphorus oxides produce only weak acids, so phosphorus does not have Property 2.

**B** is incorrect as the electron configuration of sulfur is 3p<sup>4</sup>. Sulfur has one paired 3p electron and therefore does not satisfy Property 1.

**C** is incorrect as neither element has both properties. Sulfur lacks Property 1 and phosphorus lacks Property 2.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Sulfur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>) also produces an acid when added to water:
> 
> SO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O $\rightarrow$ H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>.
> 
> However, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> is a **weak acid** and does not fully dissociate, so it does not satisfy Property 2. Only SO<sub>3</sub>, which forms the strong acid H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, satisfies Property 2.

parts.problem_md:
Period 3 elements can react with chlorine to produce the following chlorides:

MgCl<sub>2</sub>       AlCl<sub>3</sub>      SiCl<sub>4</sub>      PCl<sub>3</sub>      SCl<sub>2</sub>

Period 3 elements also react with oxygen to produce oxides.

When the oxides are produced is when the period 3 element is in its highest possible oxidation state. Which of the elements have a higher oxidation number than in the above chlorides?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The oxidation states of the Period 3 elements in the chlorides listed are:

  - MgCl<sub>2</sub> = +2
  - AlCl<sub>3</sub> = +3
  - SiCl<sub>4</sub> = +4
  - PCl<sub>3</sub> = +3
  - SCl<sub>2</sub> = +2

- The oxidation states in their **highest possible oxides** are:

  - MgO = +2
  - Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> = +3
  - SiO<sub>2</sub> = +4
  - P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> = **+5**
  - SO<sub>3</sub> = **+6**

- Only **phosphorus** (+3 → +5) and **sulfur** (+2 → +6) have higher oxidation states in their oxides than in the chlorides listed.

**A** is incorrect as Mg (+2), Al (+3), and Si (+4) have the same oxidation state in both their chlorides and their highest oxides.

**B** is incorrect as Al has oxidation state +3 in both AlCl<sub>3</sub> and Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. It is not higher in the oxide.

**C** is incorrect as Mg and Si have the same oxidation states in their oxides as in their chlorides (+2 and +4 respectively).

> **[exam-tip]**
> Phosphorus and sulfur can reach higher oxidation states in their oxides because they can use d orbitals to expand beyond an octet.
> 
> Phosphorus reaches +5 (in P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>) and sulfur reaches +6 (in SO<sub>3</sub>).
> 
> In the chlorides listed here, neither reaches its maximum oxidation state.

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: Mg, Al, Si, P and S
